subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR ACTION TO EFFECT A SETTLEMENT WITH FRED TURNER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased today to table, pursuant to Standing Order 106, a petition which is certified correct. It is from residents throughout the Northwest Territories on behalf of Mr. Fred Turner.
The petitioners hold the opinion that the Government of Canada has inflicted a severe injustice to one of its citizens by wrongfully depriving Fred Turner of his right to earn a living through the operation of his family business.
Since the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) agreed to examine the situation but has chosen instead to avoid the issue and to hide behind the courts, the petitioners call upon the House to take whatever actions possible to find an equitable settlement to assist Fred Turner and his family after this unfair and perhaps illegal loss.

subsubtopic: CANADA POST-OPPOSITION TO CLOSURE OF POST OFFICE- WILNO, ONT.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 106, it is my honour to present a petition on behalf of the residents of Wilno, Ontario, and indeed of the Canadian-Polish community of Canada at
large. Canada Post is attempting to reduce the service if not close down the post office at Wilno, Ontario, in the County of Renfrew. Wilno is the oldest community of Polish origin in Canada. The national campgrounds of the Canadian Polish community are just six miles away from the general store in Wilno where this post office is located.
The petitioners have asked me to present this petition to the Parliament of Canada asking, for heritage and historical reasons, and indeed for community service reasons, that this post office remain open and that the rural route remain as it is now and that the postmaster remain on salary so that he can handle the post office. It is very important to all these people in Canada because they come to Wilno to visit every year from all major parts of Canada.

subtopic: MUTUAL LEGAL ASSISTANCE IN CRIMINAL MATTERS ACT

speakeroldname: Hon. Ray Hnatyshyn (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MUTUAL LEGAL ASSISTANCE IN CRIMINAL MATTERS ACT
speechtext:
that Bill C-58, an Act to provide for the implementation of treaties for mutual legal assistance in criminal matters and to amend the Criminal Code, the Crown Liability Act and the Immigration Act, 1976, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, at the outset of my remarks dealing with this third important justice initiative we have considered, 1 would like to draw to the attention of the House the fact that I do appreciate very much the co-operation of the House in dealing with these matters. While they are different pieces of legislation, they are all important in their own right and deal with some tangible realities we face in today's society.
Legal Assistance
It has long been recognized that no nation can exist in isolation. Indeed, states have always regarded international cooperation as being essential to their good relations. In criminal matters, such co-operation has traditionally taken the following forms: extradition, commissioned, evidence, service of documents issued by a foreign court and informal co-operation between police forces.
These types of assistance, although still useful and necessary, were developed at a time when crimes were not normally committed beyond the boundaries of any one country. Because of the spectacular increase in means of communication and transportation, criminals are no longer inhibited by territorial boundaries. Quite the contrary, criminals take advantage of the traditional notion of territorial jurisdiction to escape detection and prosecution.
Crime is no longer a local or national affair. It is now transnational. A transnational crime can be described as a crime whose planning or execution has taken place in two or more countries. Obvious examples of such crimes would include drug trafficking, crimes associated with terrorism, tax evasion, money laundering, fraud and organized crime.
Transnational crime has become an international problem which requires a solution at an international level. Hence, the purpose of mutual legal assistance in criminal matters.
You will recall that an important treaty was signed by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and President Reagan on March 18, 1985, in Quebec City. The Bill we are dealing with today sets out the appropriate legal framework necessary to implement in Canada the provisions of the Canada-U.S. treaty on mutual legal assistance and those of any other treaty to which Canada may become a party. The Bill is not itself a code of mutual legal assistance but enables implementation of treaties.
Let me now describe what mutual legal assistance is. Simply put, it is an arrangement whereby a country, the requested state, at the request of another country, the requesting state, agrees to gather in its own territory evidence of a crime which is largely or entirely committed in the requesting state. As the words themselves imply, it must be stressed that mutual legal assistance is not a one-way street. It benefits, on a reciprocal basis, all those involved. This means Canada will obtain the same kind of assistance for Canadian investigations as we are able to provide for foreign investigations.
The new scheme encompasses every possible means of legal assistance. By way of illustration, let me read Article 2, paragraph 2 of the Canada-U.S. treaty:
Assistance shall include:
(a)	examining objects and sights;
(b)	exchanging information and objects;
(c)	locating or identifying persons;
(d)	serving documents;

September 15, 1987
Legal Assistance
(e)	taking evidence of persons;
(f)	providing documents and records;
(g)	transferring persons in custody;
(h)	executing requests for searches and seizures.
1 wish to assure all Canadians that the Bill does not open up Canadian borders to foreign police forces. Important safeguards have been developed to that effect. Foreign requests for assistance may be denied by the Minister of Justice if he or she is of the view that they are contrary to Canadian public interest. Where a foreign request for assistance is accepted, it will be executed by Canadian police officers and supervised, in the case of compulsory measures of assistance, by Canadian courts pursuant to Canadian standards and Canadian laws.
We must recognize mutual legal assistance as a tool which is both modern and essential to the fight against transnational or international crime.
Canada has chosen to base its system of mutual legal assistance on a network of bilateral treaties which will specify for each treaty partner those measures of assistance, compulsory or not, that Canada has agreed to make available, and the offences for which Canada will provide assistance. The Government is of the view that this procedure is the most appropriate because it is flexible enough to produce treaties that are tailor-made, so to speak, to the particular needs of both Canada and its treaty partner.
The Bill provides for the listing in a schedule of foreign states which have signed a mutual legal assistance treaty with Canada and the publication of such treaties in The Canada Gazette for the courts to take judicial note of. In essence, mutual legal assistance is of benefit to our own country and to the country with whom we enter into the treaty.

However the signature of a treaty does not mean that existing co-operation agreements between Canadian and foreign police forces will no longer be honoured. Quite the contrary, Mr. Speaker, the Bill expressly acknowledges that informal mutual legal assistance will be maintained; the treaty will complement it on a more official basis, but without replacing it.

It should also be noted that the treaty approach chosen by Canada will not prevent the Government from providing assistance to non-treaty countries when assistance is warranted in the international context. Indeed, where there is no treaty between Canada and another country, the Bill recognizes that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark), with agreement of the Minister of Justice, may enter into an administrative arrangement with that foreign country. Such an arrangement will be executed like a treaty and will be valid for a specific purpose and a limited period of time, not exceeding six months. This will provide Canada with the flexibility to
respond, on a case-by-case basis, to unforeseen situations of a serious nature, such as terrorist acts for which a foreign state may require Canadian assistance in uncovering evidence located in our territory. Moreover, in exceptional circumstances, administrative arrangements will also be available to treaty countries for non-listed offences when the treaty so provides.
Let me review the main provisions of the Bill. Under the Bill the responsibility for mutual legal assistance in criminal matters has been assigned to the Minister of Justice. He has been designated as the central authority for Canada. Upon receipt of the request, the Department of Justice of the requested state as central authority, if it accepts the request, is obliged to carry it out. This is done by transmittal of the request to appropriate competent authorities, that is police agencies or prosecutors, for execution according to the laws of the requested state.
As I indicated earlier, mutual legal assistance encompasses both non-compulsory and compulsory means of assistance. The Bill will only apply to compulsory assistance. There are four categories of so-called compulsory measures of assistance: search warrants, summoning of witnesses, temporary transfer of persons in custody, and the lending of Canadian exhibits to a foreign state.
The Bill sets out the procedure applicable to each of these categories of compulsory measures of assistance. These measures, however, will not be made available, as a matter of course, to every country in the world. Indeed, before a compulsory measure of assistance is made available to a foreign country several conditions will have to be met. The requesting state must be a party to a treaty with Canada. Such treaty must provide for the measure of assistance sought. The measure of assistance must be requested for an offence covered by the treaty. The request for assistance must be in conformity with provisions of the applicable treaty. The request for assistance must not be contrary to Canadian public interest as determined by the Minister of Justice. Finally, the safeguards contained in the Bill, including an order from a Canadian judge, must have been respected.
Let me now describe briefly the procedure made applicable in the Bill to the four general categories of compulsory measures of assistance, firstly with respect to the matter of the search warrant.

The Bill provides the possibility of securing in Canada a search warrant to gather information or evidence for a foreign investigation. The relevant procedure set forth in the Bill is in keeping with the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and our legal principles, and it provides strong guarantees because the search is conducted within the scope of a foreign investigation.
September 15, 1987

These safeguards are as follows. First, the application must be made to a Canadian Superior Court judge. Second, the judge must be satisfied that no other less intrusive means would be appropriate to gather the evidence sought. Third, the judge must be satisfied that an offence within the treaty was committed in the requesting state and that evidence of that offence can be found in Canada.
If the judge is satisfied that these conditions are met and issues a search warrant, it must be executed by a Canadian peace officer named in the warrant. The person who has been the object of the search may make representations to the judge who issued the warrant either to have it set aside or to request that before the things seized are sent abroad conditions be imposed in respect of the rights of owners or third parties and with respect to the preservation and return of these things to Canada.
In that regard, because the Canadian judge has no jurisdiction over the foreign country, the Bill also provides that no object or thing will be sent abroad until the Minister of Justice is satisfied that the foreign state will respect the conditions imposed by the Canadian judge.
Dealing with the evidence-gathering order provisions of the Bill, the purpose of this judicial order is to compel a person to testify or to produce a record, document or other article. Again, provision is made for terms and conditions to be imposed by the judge, including the manner in which a refusal by the witness to answer questions is to be dealt with where such refusal is based on a law in force in Canada or in the requesting state.
In a nutshell, Mr. Speaker, where the objection is based on a law in force in Canada it will be decided by the judge. However, if the objection relates to a possible breach of a privilege recognized by a law in force in the requesting state, or to a possible breach of a criminal provision in force in the foreign state, the objection will be taken down in writing and will be sent to the requesting state for decision. If the objection is overruled, the witness will be obliged to answer. If he still persists in his refusal he could then, of course, be guilty of contempt of court.
It is worth mentioning at this point that both the search warrant and the evidence-gathering order will also be available to gather information which may reveal the whereabouts of a person who is suspected of having committed an offence covered by the treaty.
Dealing with the provisions concerning transfer of persons in custody, the Bill would allow the temporary transfer of a detained person from a Canadian jail to a foreign country for the purpose of testifying or helping in an investigation. Such a transfer will only take place with the express consent of the detained person. It should also be mentioned that young
Legal Assistance
persons within the meaning of the Young Offenders Act will not be subject to transfer even if they consent.
Measures are provided to ensure that the detention of the Canadian inmate in a foreign country does not imperil his or her rights with respect to any remission which would have accrued to him or her had it not been for the transfer to a foreign country. Conversely, when a foreign prisoner is transferred to Canada pursuant to a Canadian request for assistance, provisions have been made for his or her entry into Canada, his or her continued detention, and his or her return to the requested country.
Moving to the provisions with respect to the lending of exhibits, exhibits that have been admitted in evidence in a criminal proceeding in Canada would be lent to a foreign state if the court which has possession of the exhibits so orders. If a loan order is made it would be subjected to several conditions in respect of a test to be performed on the exhibits, its preservation and its return to Canada. Again, since the court has no jurisdiction over the foreign state, no loan order will be made until the court is satisfied that the foreign state has agreed to the conditions.
Besides setting out the procedures applicable to the compulsory measures of assistance, the Bill allows foreign states to apply to Canadian courts to enforce payment of fines imposed in criminal matters in those countries. It contains provisions to protect foreign records sent to Canada pursuant to a Canadian request by creating a privilege for those records until such records are made public or are admitted in evidence in compliance with the conditions on which they were sent to Canada.
The Bill also contains a consequential amendment which would authorize Canadian police officers to disclose to a foreign police force or prosecutor private communications which have been intercepted in Canada if such disclosure is intended to be in the best interests of the administration of justice.
I must underline why I have described the provisions with respect to the operation within Canada. That is for the purpose of understanding the provisions of the Bill because they are reciprocal. Accordingly, the same measures of assistance which are made available to a foreign state in the execution of search warrants, evidence gathering, lending of exhibits, and the transfer of detained persons will also be made available to Canadian authorities by the foreign state as a recognition of its treaty obligations toward Canada.

Finally, Mr. Speaker, I do not think it is necessary to lay more emphasis on the importance of the legislative measures I am tabling today. They will provide Canada with a legal framework whose scope will enable us to respond efficiently to the ever present and growing threats of terrorism and international drug trafficking, while at the same time giving us

September 15, 1987
Legal Assistance
sufficient leeway to be in a position to implement the provisions of the Canada/United States treaty and any other similar treaty which Canada might negotiate in the future with a common law or civil right country,

I am confident that this Bill, in conjunction with mutual legal assistance treaties, will enhance the existing co-operation between Canada and other nations and is a major step forward in Canada's efforts to deal effectively with international crime.
This Bill provides the framework for important advances in law enforcement in our country. As I said at the outset, international and transnational crime is, regrettably, very much in existence. 1 believe this legislation is a responsible approach to questions of mutual legal assistance. We are now moving toward a legislative framework which will be available for the protection of Canadian citizens and will allow for procedures to be put in place and the scrutiny of our own courts in the case of applications by those foreign states with which we have treaties.
On the other hand, Canadians will be the beneficiaries because we know that in order to prosecute successfully serious crimes under our criminal code it becomes more and more necessary in today's society for us to acquire foreign evidence. This Bill will provide us with the framework for that inasmuch as we will not have to rely on the goodwill of foreign law enforcement agencies. Under the provisions of this Bill and the treaties which accompany it we will have the ability to obtain evidence in other countries to assist our prosecutors to prosecute successfully crimes which were committed within our territory, therefore serving the interests of justice in our country.
1 have always been a great believer in having these matters spelled out in the law of the land. In that way parliamentarians can ensure that safeguards for our citizens are included. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, to Members of the House and to Canadians in general that we must take these steps nowadays in order to ensure that we in Canada have the tools available to us to attack successfully the international trafficking of drugs and organized crime which knows no boundaries but operates transnationally. We have to take these steps in order to enhance our ability to serve the Canadian public through our law enforcement agencies, by providing them with the best tools available in order to prosecute illicit and illegal activity in our country.
1 ask that Members of the House give this legislation favourable consideration so that we can move forward to the committee stage and examine the provisions of the Bill, and in the final analysis be able to serve our fellow citizens by bringing forward legislation that will best serve the interest of proper law enforcement in Canada.

subtopic: MUTUAL LEGAL ASSISTANCE IN CRIMINAL MATTERS ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister made compassioned concluding remarks with a perfectly
straight face. I will open in the same vein and take him out of his suspense and agony by indicating that Her Majesty's Official Opposition intends to support this Bill in principle.
We support the Bill in principle, although I refer to the Minister's straight face because I think it has to be acknowledged that this legislation is largely a public relations exercise by the Government. It results from an agreement at the Shamrock Summit to the effect that mutual assistance in police matters and criminal investigations would be undertaken between Canada and the United States.
While the treaty was signed in Quebec City, perhaps the Minister could correct me now if my understanding is wrong that the treaty has not been ratified by the American Congress and is not yet in effect in the United States. However, here we are, not only with a treaty which is in effect, because it is binding in Canada without ratification, but with legislation that is brought forward by the Government to give effect to the important measures that will improve Canada's ability to assist other countries in the war against crime.
The Minister also ought to recognize that virtually all of the measures which this Bill provides for by way of legislation are already part of the practice in our country- primarily established by judicial orders-and well known in the common law and in the civil law in every province. This Bill legislates things that are already provided for in Canadian law, although not until now provided for in Canadian statute law.
On behalf of the Official Opposition I want to indicate that we are in favour of this legislative advance in principle. We hope that the United States takes this treaty as seriously as the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) and ratifies the treaty as well and proceeds to introduce similar legislation. It seems that this is another one of those cases where the Americans do not take those things agreed to as seriously-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MUTUAL LEGAL ASSISTANCE IN CRIMINAL MATTERS ACT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. The Hon. Member asked me to correct him if he was wrong in his assumption. The American process is somewhat different than ours. We are in fact dealing with this matter by legislation. They do not require the same legislative route in order to ratify the treaty. Before we are in a position to properly bring about the effect of this treaty, we require legislation to be presented in the House. The Americans have indicated that they are prepared, through their own procedures, to ratify it as soon as we are in a position to move forward with the passage of legislation.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: MUTUAL LEGAL ASSISTANCE IN CRIMINAL MATTERS ACT
speechtext: Since that has been clarified, we can carry on with the Member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan).

subtopic: MUTUAL LEGAL ASSISTANCE IN CRIMINAL MATTERS ACT
speechtext:
Recently the President of the United States set out his vision for his remaining term of office. I noted his remarks with interest, and the ratification of this treaty and the bringing in of legislation to give effect to it was not mentioned, nor was the Conservative Government free trade
September 15, 1987

initiative. My point is that we are taking this matter seriously even if the Americans do not. Let me indicate that we approve of that.
The Minister indicated that legislation is necessary to implement the treaty. While that is true, certainly no legislation is needed to give effect to any of the types of procedures that are now going to be provided for by legislation. As the Minister knows, we already have extradition procedures and a well developed common law system by which the four types of assistance that are provided for in this legislation are already available.
I want to express my concerns, which I will enlarge upon when the measure goes to committee. I hope at that time we will be able to get satisfactory answers.
One must begin with the principle that any measures that will assist in law enforcement and in the war against crime, international crime or organized crime, are welcome and ought to be supported. Certainly we will do so. We can begin by providing for this assistance between Canada and the United States because there are no two stronger allies than Canada and the United States. However, I would remind the House that even in our relations with the United States there are crimes to which they take a different attitude than do we.
I am glad to say that the law reserves the discretion on the Canadian side to decide how far we want to go in helping the United States achieve their law enforcement objectives. We do not have the same criminal laws as the United States. We do not have the same foreign policy in every respect as they do. Our law must take account of that and therefore it does not provide for automatic assistance.
An example of this is the draft dodger situation that arises between Canada and the United States every few decades, hopefully less often in the future than in the past. At the beginning of World War II, Canadians went to the United States and were immune from being extradited back to Canada to be punished for not fighting in our war. Similarly, during the Vietnam war when Americans came to Canada to escape the draft in that country, whether or not we welcomed them, we certainly provided a haven for them from prosecution in the United States provided they met our immigration standards.
In our opinion, even the American justice system, as fine and admirable as it is, sometimes goes astray. That happened in the Peltier case, where a Canadian Indian is in the United States being punished for a crime, when in our opinion false evidence had admittedly been used to obtain his conviction. We have a different view of the situation than the Americans. We want to be certain that signing a treaty and passing a statute does not simply mean we will be delivering people to the United States to fit in with their foreign policy priorities and their criminal law system, as much as we admire them.
I think also of the FLQ incidents in which the United States is currently seeking extradition of airplane hijackers whom we
Legal Assistance
know as the FLQ, 18 years after the fact. It is important in such a situation that it be our system of justice that makes a Canadian decision about whether and how far we propose to co-operate with the United States.
Finally, when considering our relations with the United States I think the issue of the death penalty must bear on the considerations of the Government about extradition to the United States. We recently decided in this Chamber that the death penalty is not an acceptable punishment for even the most serious crimes. In the United States literally hundreds of people are convicted and are awaiting execution. If requests come to us from the United States for candidates for eventual execution under the criminal justice system of the United States-and I am not saying we should automatically oppose it because I do not feel we should-I believe in those circumstances a Canadian decision will have to be made and this treaty and legislation should not be taken as a waiver of the Canadian interest in cases like that.
I examined some other circumstances involving Canada and third countries, because this legislation, while it relates to the Shamrock Summit agreement, has a wider scope. It will permit Canada to sign mutual assistance treaties with other countries in the world and provide assistance to them in law enforcement objectives. I would like to say that there are many countries with which we would have a law enforcement interest, and I am thinking about drugs, evasion of family responsibilities, escaping with children, a marriage to a person from a third country-there are many reasons why it is in the interests of Canada to have treaties with other countries. However, we must at the same time remember that in respect of many of the countries with which we would want to cooperate on police matters, in some cases, there are very good reasons to be extremely guarded.
Recently, for example, there was a request from Argentina to extradite a florist living in Canada for the murder of his wife which occurred 11 years ago. I would urge that in a case like that, where we would want a murderer to be returned to face the music for what he did, we should bear in mind that there could be a political dimension to the demand. He may well have a defence that he would not be allowed to make, or could not freely make, even in a democracy like Argentina, or in Chile, or in other countries with which we have a police interest, in many ways, but where there is such a fundamental differences in values to those in our system of government and in our definition of dissent and protest.
While we might sign a treaty, we would only do so if we could be very certain that a Canadian standard of respect for fundamental human rights and values would be part of the consideration of the government. That would have to be a consideration with respect to how far we wanted to play ball with these countries in achieving what they would characterize as a straightforward law enforcement or anti-criminal objective.

September 15, 1987
Legal Assistance
We would want to be certain, in connection with all of these treaty countries, that confidential information would not be made public and not be transferred to countries except in very circumscribed and controlled situations. When we think about it, the Government of Canada has access in its records, and in related records, by computers and so on, to the most intimate details of the private life of every person in this country; if they have had an abortion, if they have been bankrupt or failed to pay ordinary private debts, if they have had mental problems or complaints against them by neighbours, justified or unjustified. All of this information is becoming easily accessible in relation to every individual within our borders.
That pool of information, which is not even available, or should not be available, to other Canadians or other Canadian agencies, should certainly not now suddenly become available to foreign governments which might want to abuse it or which might not have the same kind of safeguards we have to ensure that the information is not used to violate the privacy of an individual for no good purpose at all.

In conclusion, although I may have sounded rather negative I should like to emphasize that the Official Opposition will support the Bill under consideration. Still I express our concern over the fact that the measure relates to a field of individual privacy, that it affects the property of probably just about anybody in this country; we want to make sure that the Government is very much aware of these values, that the treaty or the legislation will give us free reign to restrict the access of foreigners to our citizenship and to individuals in this country.
That being said, Mr. Speaker, again I offer our support and express our interest in seeing this piece of legislation adopted in due time. We endorse this measure.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as already explained by the Hon. Member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan), this Bill stems from the March 1985 treaty signed in Quebec City by Ronald Reagan and our Prime Minister at the so-called Shamrock Summit. We in the New Democratic Party know very well that a number of agreements signed and advocated during that summit are not in the interest of Canadians. For this reason, of course, we are acutely aware of our responsibility to scrutinize the treaty which has just been signed concerning the exchange of information between the United States and Canada, not only between the United States and Canada but also, as indicated in this measure, with other as yet unnamed countries. As the Hon. Member for York Centre pointed out, we want to know exactly which other countries we are talking about because, on the strength of Clause 4 of the Bill, for instance, it will be left to the Government or the Governor in Council, meaning Cabinet, to add other countries covered under this Bill. As we see it, such a decision might indeed have an impact on the civil liberties of Canadians and it must be made by Parliament, not only by the Government or Cabinet.

Recognizing that this legislation flows from the treaty which was signed in March of 1985 by Ronald Reagan, the President of the United States, and the Canadian Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), and recognizing as well the extent to which the Canadian Prime Minister, the head of the Conservative Government, has been prepared to cede fundamental aspects of Canadian sovereignty, we naturally are concerned; we are concerned about the implications of legislation which flows from that Shamrock Summit.
There is a broader question here. The Liberal justice critic has said we have some concerns about this Bill, but we like it and will support it in principle. However, when we start to examine carefully, not only the legislation itself but more importantly the history of the Government's negotiations with the United States, its failure to stand up for the interests of Canadians, then surely we must recognize the potential for serious abuse of the civil liberties, rights and privacy of Canadians which exists with respect to this legislation.
I would like to say a few words about the Government's failure to negotiate on behalf of Canadians, its failure to take effective action in dealing with the United States to protect Canadians from the laws and policies of the United States which are manifestly unjust and work to the detriment of our people here in Canada. Let me give two examples and ask why the Government of Canada and its Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) are prepared to give significant new powers to United States law enforcement officers without insisting, on behalf of Canadians, on action in other areas?
One of those areas is the provision of American legislation in the area of immigration. I refer here to the provisions of the McCarran-Walter Act. This is a United States law which was basically passed at the height of the cold war in the 1950s. It is a law which has been used to bar Canadian citizens from visiting the United States.
Who are these dangerous, subversive citizens who have been denied entry to the United States, denied even the right to pass through the United States as a result of this piece of legislation that is so reprehensible and constitutes such a denial of the civil liberties, not only of Canadians but of all others who would seek to visit the United States?
One of those dangerous subversives is a Canadian author named Farley Mowat. Under the provisions of the McCarran-Walter Act, this United States law which is still on the books today, Farley Mowat was told that he could not enter the United States to promote a book he had written. He wanted to board a Los Angeles-bound flight in Toronto in 1985. At that time the American authorities told him that the door was closed to him.
Why was the door closed to Farley Mowat? In 1968, in a jocular and offhand manner, Farley Mowat threatened to shoot down U.S. aircraft flying through Canadian air space.
September 15, 1987

As a result of that joke, which clearly is all it was, he was denied the right to enter the United States. In fact, this American law, and the discretionary powers under it, have been used to stifle debate by denying entry to foreigners, including Canadians, whose views do not necessarily coincide with the views of the American Government.
There was also another person, a person from Saskatchewan, who was denied entry to the United States as well under the provisions of the McCarran-Walter Act. I refer to a professor from the University of Regina School of Human Justice, a professor named Jim Harding, a good friend of the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom). He is obviously a dangerous radical and a subversive. He was denied the right to even pass through the United States en route to a United Nations conference in Costa Rica.
Why was that? Why was Professor Jim Harding turned away by U.S. immigration officials in Calgary when he wanted to board a flight for Mexico via Los Angeles? He was told that he was on a list of Canadians who were not admissible to the United States. He asked the Americans for an explanation. He asked why it was that he could not even pass through the United States en route to a conference. He was told that apparently the American authorities considered him to be a communist because in 1961 he had attended a conference on disarmament in the Soviet Union with a number of other Canadian students.
I remind Hon. Members that this incident of being refused entry to the United States occurred at the beginning of this year. Also attending that conference were people such as Lord Bertrand Russell and Jean-Paul Sartre. Because of that law which still exists in the United States Professor Jim Harding, who has a long and distinguished involvement in the peace movement, was refused the right even to pass through the United States in transit to Central America.
What did the Canadian Department of External Affairs do to stand up for the rights of this Canadian? It did not do anything at all. It said that it regretted the incident but it respects the sovereign right of the United States to decide who can come and go in that country. That type of kowtowing to legislation which is reprehensible and which denies Canadians the right to visit the United States, or even to pass through it, that type of knuckling under is clearly not acceptable to those of us in this Party. Our Government should be saying to Ronald Reagan, look, Ronnie, if you want new powers under the mutual legal assistance legislation you are going to have to do something about a law which has been on the books of your country since 1950, a law which has denied access to your country to Farley Mowat, to Professor Jim Harding, and to many other Canadians, a law which is being used and has been used to stifle political debate, a law which poses a threat to international scholarship.
We say that if the Government wants to extend new powers to the United States to engage in investigative activity in
Legal Assistance
Canada then let it do some tough-minded and serious negotiation, let it tell the Americans that we do not accept this outdated and dangerous law. Let the Government tell the Americans that they owe an apology to the Canadians who have been excluded from the United States as a result of this law and that we are not prepared to co-operate with them in the manner in which they are now seeking unless they take steps to deal with this matter.
There is an opportunity for the Government to act. United States Congressman Barney Frank from Massachusetts has a Bill before the American Congress that would in fact repeal the most repugnant provisions of this legislation.
I suggest that the Government and the Prime Minister go back to the bargaining table to suggest to the President of the United States that if he wants our co-operation in this area then how about some co-operation in supporting the legislation that is before the United States Congress today to get rid of it? That is the first point. Let us have some serious negotiations here instead of just giving in to the Americans, as the Government has done on so many issues in the past, and as it is continuing to do, we fear, in the free trade negotiations.
One other example of actions which could and should have been taken by the Government in the context of negotiation of this treaty is looking at the question of one of the most serious abuses of the rights of Canadians citizens by American authorities. I am talking here about the psychic brainwashing experiments that were carried out by the CIA in the late 1950s and early 1960s. These were experiments that used Canadians as human guinea pigs, experiments in mind control that were carried out by Dr. Ewen Cameron at the Allan Memorial Institute in Montreal. We know the tragic history of this particular series of events. Cameron, in researching brainwashing techniques, took advantage of men and women, primarily women. Three-quarters of his victims were women. He took advantage of people who came to him as a doctor, people who were depressed and in need of psychiatric help. Instead of helping those people he used them in his grisly mind control experiments without informing them that that is what he was doing.
This research was dreamed up at the height of the cold war in the United States. The CIA was funding this research. One of the victims of these terrible experiments was the wife of the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow), one of the best known victims. She was subjected to the following treatment by Dr. Ewen Cameron. She was subjected to a taped message being repeated over and over and over again which told her, "You are a bad mother. You are a bad wife". To this day, of course, she feels the effects of that type of experimentation. The coalition that has been attempting to seek justice and compensation for these people alleges that some others were not as lucky. They have committed suicide. Most cannot work. One of the victims has died. Many others are permanently scarred by these terrible experiments.

September 15, 1987
Legal Assistance
What is the Government of Canada doing to stand up on behalf of these Canadians who were the victims of these terrible experiments? The Conservative Government appointed a former Conservative Member of Parliament from Nova Scotia to conduct a study into the implications of this particular matter. But that study was nothing less than a complete whitewash. He came to the conclusion that there was no proof that anyone was damaged by the experiments. In fact, in arriving at his conclusion he did not even speak to a single victim of the experiments. He said that the Canadian Government had no responsibility toward these victims. We fundamentally disagree.
We believe that the Government of Canada should release all the information it possesses to the victims of those experiments to assist them in their lawsuit against the CIA in the United States. We are also insisting that Canada should financially assist the victims of these brainwashing experiments. For some time we have been waiting for the Government to live up to the promise it made, that at the very least it would help these people pay for their legal expenses in bringing action against the CIA.
It is thanks to the tremendous dedication, courage, and unflagging commitment of their United States attorney, Joseph Rauh, that this action is still alive before the United States courts. But the Canadians who are pursuing this action are still waiting for the Government to live up to its promise to assist them financially in pursuing their lawsuit.
I put a question to the Minister of Justice in June, and the Minister stated that he was in the process of consulting, looking at this matter, and that he hoped to be able to come forward with some concrete results in the very near future. That was four months ago, and still no action has been taken on the part of the Government.
I wish to link this to the Bill before the House at this time, and to ask the Government, whether the Prime Minister of Canada said to his good friend, Ronald Reagan, look, Ronnie, we are going to give you some new powers under the Mutual Legal Assistance Act, but your Government, and your intelligence agency, the CIA, is still refusing to recognize its responsibility to compensate the victims of experiments by the CIA in Canada during the late 1950s? Did our Prime Minister stand up for these Canadians? Did he say that if the United States wanted these new powers, it was not going to receive them unless the Americans accepted their moral, ethical, and legal responsibility to compensate these victims?
We do not know what happened at the Shamrock conference. We do know that the victims of these experiments have so far received absolutely no assistance whatsoever from the Government of Canada. Until the Government comes to grips with this serious question and recognizes its responsibility to our citizens who are the victims of these brainwashing experiments by the CIA without their consent, why should we
co-operate in granting new powers to the Government of the United States?
Let us say to the American authorities, the Attorney General of the United States, and the President of the United States, if you wish these new powers it is about time that you took action to assist us. That is the type of hard-headed, tough negotiating that we believe should have been undertaken, and that we believe was not undertaken before this Act was brought forward.
It may well be that this is another little bone that is being tossed to the American Government as part of the price that we pay for free trade in Canada, together with the legislation on generic drugs, and the Minister of Communications knuckling under on the Broadcasting Act. I could go on with a litany of areas in which the Government has caved in to the Americans. We are afraid that perhaps this Bill is part of that pattern of knuckling under to United States pressure. We do not believe we should be giving in to that pressure. We certainly believe that Canada should be standing up for Canadians.
There are a number of other areas of concern with respect to this legislation. First, I wish to point out that the Liberal spokesperson indicated that the Liberal Party intends to support this Bill in principle. Once again the Liberals and the Conservatives are in bed together on a matter that fundamentally affects the rights and sovereignty of Canadians. The Liberal justice critic said that this Bill is simply implementing what is presently being done informally. Quite obviously the Liberal justice critic has not read the Bill, if that is the position that he has taken. There are at least two significant elements of this Bill which do extend the powers of the United States investigative authorities.
The new Canada-United States treaty which would come into effect as a result of this Bill would allow the collection of evidence in Canada by United States police at a far earlier stage than is presently permitted. Presently under Canadian law the United States enforcement agencies are only permitted to seek Canadian co-operation in the gathering of evidence after charges have been laid, or after a trial has begun in the United States. The Prime Minister is now saying, come on in even before charges have been laid. We will allow you to investigate, and to use all of the powers in this new Act under this new treaty at the investigation stage. That is a significant change. It is not just putting into effect something which is informally taking place now, because if it is informally taking place now Canadian laws are being broken.
Another element in which this changes the law, and not just putting into effect a law which is already utilized in practice, as the Liberal justice critic has suggested, is the extent to which currently Canadian legislation denies American police access to search warrants for wholly foreign offences which are committed in the United States. This law would also change that.
September 15, 1987

What are the types of offences we are talking about here? We do not have to go back too far to find instances of Americans being guilty of offences in the United States who came to Canada and when, fortunately, we said that we were not prepared to turn our backs on those Americans, but rather we welcomed them. They were Americans who did not want to participate in fighting an immoral war in Vietnam. They came to Canada in large numbers. In doing so, they were breaking American laws.
Under the provisions of this treaty, and particularly this legislation, the Canadian Government would be involved. The Canadian police forces and the RCMP would be involved in helping authorities in the United States bring those people before American courts. I do not believe we should be involved in that type of thing. I do not believe we should be involved in a situation in which Americans who are seeking to assist refugees fleeing from Central America should be subject to investigation by Canadian authorities working hand in hand with the FBI. I do not believe that Americans who are seeking to peacefully protest American policy in Central America, and who subsequently may come to Canada, should be subject to investigation by Canadian authorities at the instance of the American police.
Last week in a hospital in Walnut Creek, California, I visited a very courageous and dedicated young man named Brian Willson. He is a veteran of the war in Vietnam. He realizes the immorality of that war, and has dedicated his life to doing what he can to ensure that the United States does not participate in other immoral, unjust military actions. Along with a number of other American men and women, Brian Willson peacefully demonstrated outside the Concord naval weapons base, in Concord, California. They gave notice to the naval authorities that they intended to peacefully erect a banner and stand by that banner on the train tracks which were transporting weapons to Central America, which ultimately may very well have been used by the Contras in their murderous attacks on civilians in Nicaragua.
Brian Willson was run down by a naval train carrying weapons as he peacefully demonstrated. He lost both legs and fractured his skull. In engaging in that act of peaceful civil disobedience he did break American law.
I do not want Canada to be helping the United States authorities prosecute the Brian Willsons of the United States should they come to Canada. I do not want to see Canada assisting the FBI in ferreting out refugees who are fleeing from Central America and who seek sanctuary in Canada. 1 do not believe that Canadian law should be used in a manner that would subvert all of the finest traditions and principles of Canadian justice. I do not believe that Canadian law should be used to assist in the gathering of evidence in a manner that may indeed involve serious invasions of the privacy of Canadians.
Legal Assistance
Under this law there will be access to a wide-ranging array of information. A most important point is that this legislation does not just deal with the United States, but would allow the Canadian Government to enter into similar treaties or agreements with any other country in the world. The Government does not even have to come back to Parliament to do so. Once the Cabinet decides it wants to enter into such an agreement, it merely passes an Order in Council, and that is it.
What if this Government of Canada or a future Government decided it wanted to pass a similar agreement with say a brutal military junta similar to the one governing Chile today? Such an agreement could facilitate the very serious abuse of the rights of Chileans who have sought refuge in Canada from that bloody dictatorship. We know already that Canada's CSIS is co-operating in a shameful way with the Chilean intelligence agency, the CNI.
I do not want to be responsible for the passage of a piece of legislation that ultimately could lead to Canada co-operating with military regimes in Chile or elsewhere, co-operating with police forces against citizens who have sought refuge in this country. Fifteen Chilean are possibly subject to the death penalty as a result of certain allegations. Those trials have taken place under a system of military justice which denies all of the basic rights accorded under any sensible and decent system of justice. If one of those people were to show up in Canada, I would hope that Canada would not co-operate in the manner envisaged by this legislation in sending these people back.
This Bill is wrong in principle because of the possible dangers it poses, not just to Canadians but to people from other countries who may seek refuge in Canada and who may have committed acts recognized as offences in those jurisdictions, but by no means offences that we may want to involve ourselves with in Canada.
Obviously when we are talking about co-operation respecting offences involving organized crime, that is another question and Canada should extend its fullest possible co-operation in those areas. But this legislation, Mr. Speaker, is dangerous because it has the potential to go far, far beyond that.
Because of the reasons I have outlined, because of the failure of the Government to stand up for Canadians-and before adopting this legislation we should insist upon the Americans taking their obligations seriously concerning the victims of the CIA brainwashing experiments and the McCar-ran-Walter Act-and because of serious concerns about the substance of this legislation and the potential of very grave abuse of civil liberties in Canada, we in the New Democratic Party are strongly opposed to this Bill and will be opposing it in principle. The Government should go back to the drawing-board, go back to the Americans and insist on justice.

Mr. Speaker, I will speak to my colleagues about this massive breach of etiquette in the House of Commons. One of our colleagues from the other side of the House seems to want to speak. Undoubtedly she will speak on this Bill; we will listen breathless and spellbound to her contributions.
1 would like to offer congratulations to my colleague, the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson), who expressed some very serious concerns in a number of areas about the legislation before the House today. First, is Canada negotiating effectively with the United States in the development of the number of treaties and arrangements that we have seen come through the House? He gave examples to show that the answer is no.
In the minds of most Members of this House on all sides, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) of Canada has involved himself in a massive giveaway. To the Americans, without question and without an attempt to negotiate, have gone such things as the salmon interception treaty on the West Coast and the present legislation before us today. In the minds of most Canadians the Conservative Government and the Prime Minister are involved in a massive giveaway in an attempt to secure a free trade agreement. It is time that we as Canadians dug in and began to negotiate effectively.
This Parliament should not pass this Bill without changes. The Prime Minister should be digging in his heels with the Americans on the question of the salmon interception treaty on the West Coast. We have no effective authority over our resources in the Yukon River. That was an omission. The problem was known but we heard that it might offend the Americans and the President if we began to ask for things that belonged to us and which might jeopardize the free trade agreement.
There were the summit meetings between the Prime Minister and the United States President. Instead of dealing effectively with Canadian resources in the transboundary rivers that cross southeast Alaska flowing into the Province of British Columbia, which rivers contain large fish stock originating in Canadian waters, the Prime Minister gave those away without a thought. In addition, we have a very poor interception agreement with the United States.
At the present time Canadians are losers in this massive giveaway in the attempt to obtain a free trade agreement with the United States. The legislation presently before the House is another example of failure to negotiate effectively. We are involved in other serious matters of negotiations with the United States, and we could use this Bill and the arrangements as leverage. 1 am speaking of what is called the A-B line, the boundary between Canada and the United States, between southeast Alaska and British Columbia. There have been numerous provocations in that disputed area by the U.S. Coast Guard. The U.S. Coast Guard has arrested Canadian fishermen, seized their catches and hauled them into court in Ketchikan, Alaska, in a completely unjust manner. Canadian fishermen who had been fishing in areas designated on Canadian maps as being Canadian territory have been arrested by the U.S. Coast Guard, hauled into Ketchikan, Alaska, and had their catches seized. There have been a great many threats of violence against them.
If the Prime Minister of Canada were fulfilling his obligations to Canadians, he would be raising these matters with the American President and suggesting that proper processes be used by the Americans in disputes. We would be prepared to co-operate with the Americans in many areas of legitimate negotiations if in fact their behaviour in certain areas was acceptable.
As well, the Americans gave petroleum leases across the AB line in absolute rejection of anything that would seem reasonable. Yet it seems we did not raise any kind of concern about that at the Shamrock Summit. No, indeed, the Prime Minister of Canada is quite prepared to give away points on the salmon interception treaty and quite prepared to fail to observe the kinds of infractions that are going on in the northwest corner of British Columbia over the A-B line.
We do not negotiate with the United States. The Conservative Government and the Prime Minister and, indeed, the past Liberal Government have virtually given away Canadian rights and Canadian sovereignty without raising substantial efforts at negotiation. This is the record, and I think it was shown effectively by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Burnaby, when he spoke today. He pointed out that this is a result of a treaty which is a give-away and that we as Canadians under the present Conservative Government are being badly served in our negotiations with the United States.
The legislation before the House assists in law enforcement matters. It was pointed out that this legislation is too far reaching and allows the involvement of law-enforcement procedures from a foreign country in Canada too early. The Hon. Member pointed out the problems involved with having demands for investigative action taking place in Canada before charges are laid, a new item over which there is concern.
September 15, 1987

As well, he pointed out that under the present legislation certain regimes will probably come forward since the legislation envisions a wider view of which countries can obtain these benefits in Canada. He pointed to the cases of Chile and Argentina. The Hon. Member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan) as well pointed out that these regimes could approach Canada and ask for law-enforcement activity within Canada targeted against individuals whose activities would not be considered criminal in Canada.
For example, there are a great many Canadians of Chilean origin, many of whom were judged to have committed crimes in that country which are not crimes in this country. They fear that regime and have been subjected to severe repression. Ultimately, the thought of our law-enforcement agencies cooperating in any way with that regime is absolutely intolerable.
As far as my colleagues and I are concerned, when this legislation goes to committee it will be given very serious scrutiny. We will look to tightening the legislation so that it is targeted at specific areas of concern. We will be very careful with any rights it allows foreign law-enforcement agencies in Canada.
There is a positive side to this legislation that I am surprised has not been discussed or has not been envisioned by the Government. Some Canadians have asked Canadian law enforcement agencies to become more involved with American law enforcement agencies in the search for missing persons, family members who have disappeared. In this case, there seems to be a great reluctance on the part of the Americans to participate effectively with Canadian authorities. It has become a matter of concern for individuals in my constituency where there is not good co-operation with American authorities in assisting in attempts to reunite family members.
In the search for missing children, law-enforcement agencies are the effective agencies. I believe this Bill could be used to encourage the United States by indicating we would certainly be prepared to assist here if we could see a much larger initiative in assistance from them.
As well, there are people who have gone to the United States to avoid family obligations imposed by Canadian courts. Assistance in solving that problem could definitely be improved by this legislation. Given the concerns in respect of those issues which exist on all sides of the House and certainly on both sides of the border, that should be looked into.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for Burnaby, mentioned a matter of serious concern on which the Canadian Government should take the initiative with the American Government. The Canadian Government should suggest that the list of excluded Canadians under the McCarran-Walter Act should be reexamined. Indeed, some of the absolutely frivolous reasons for excluding Canadians from the United States should be removed. Those Canadians should have the right to go back and forth across the boundary. Many people who live in Canada have family, contacts and friends in the United States. It becomes a very serious matter when a family member is
Legal Assistance
excluded. At least half of my own family are citizens of the United States.
During the Vietnam war, many people who lived in the United States were severely tested by the war and were under pressure of the draft and their absolute abhorrence of that war. Many were likely candidates to avoid the draft by coming to Canada. Those who did are now unable to visit immediate members of their families in the United States.
This legislation is of particular concern to me. I personally would like to see it made much tighter. Although it does not apply in my particular case, I can understand the concerns of other people over the McCarran-Walter Act. They are unable to visit family members or travel in the United States for the most absolutely frivolous reasons. It is a time both Governments approached this from a reasonable point of view and eliminated that list.
We as Members of the House of Commons know of a very tragic example of the failure of the Canadian Government to pressure, through the negotiation process, a quid pro quo approach to the question of the LSD experiments. We should indicate to the United States that we will move on areas that are of interest and concern to Americans if they will address the things that concern us as Canadians. This must be done.
The LSD experiments are an example of something that was intolerable. Great damage was done and compensation must be addressed. That issue should have been raised by the Prime Minister. There should have been a clear-cut agreement that that matter will be resolved and put to rest.
I believe we should pursue these issues as we consider the legislation through committee and report stages and on to third reading. Quite honestly, I think American officials should be invited to appear before the committee to tell us why these other items have not been addressed if we are expected to pass this legislation.
The timing of the legislation has been mentioned as an issue. The United States has not passed reciprocal legislation. In the case of the salmon interception agreement we had to make amendments to our legislation before the Americans would consider passing theirs. We do not know what they will do with their legislation. They may amend it or reject it outright. It would be better to have agreements which are worked out between Canada and the U.S. considered and ratified simultaneously and avoid this problem.
The matter before us today is of very serious concern. The Liberal Party appears prepared to move ahead quickly on this legislation. I know it was probably a slip of the tongue, but the Hon. Member for York Centre said he could see some problems when the Government was faced with requests for law enforcement assistance in Canada from democracies like Argentina and Chile. I was quite shocked when I heard that. It would be a simple matter for the Hon. Member to check and

The failure of the previous Liberal Government to negotiate effectively with the U.S. is clearly evident when we have matters such as this before us. My colleague from Burnaby indicated that in this situation the Liberals and Conservatives were largely in Bed together on their failure to negotiate effectively with the U.S. Yet it is to the credit of the previous Government that we did not see a sell-out on such a massive scale as we see with the present Government in its effort to obtain a free trade agreement. Canadians are not prepared to see that continue. If you look at the polls you can see that the record of the Government is very dismal in the eyes of Canadians. How can we become more effective in recovering missing children on both sides of the border? How can we apply the strength of our law enforcement agencies and bring in other resources in support of them? When this legislation goes to committee those are items I would like to see raised. I intend to pursue the matter vigorously through our critic, or directly if I participate on the committee. It is a logical place to do it and I would hope other Members with the same experience will pursue it as well.
Another aspect of that same problem is the situation where a parent has obligations imposed by the courts for maintenance of the family and then moves to the U.S. For all intents and purposes that could be defined as criminal activity, because that person is failing to live up to an obligation imposed by the court. I think arrangements to deal with that problem should be pursued. Probably every Member of this House has had experience at one time or another with that kind of situation. It is almost futile to pursue it unless the individual involved has a large amount of money. This particular legislative mechanism would be appropriate in dealing with that problem as well. That is an item which I would like to flag for attention in committee in order that the legislation can be expanded or made more precise to include this matter.
I am not certain which incidents in British Columbia the Member speaks about, but a number come to mind in which law enforcement co-operation between the two countries has been a little too informal and may need some legislative action. The FBI in Seattle has phoned the RCMP in Vancouver asking them to pick up and drop off in Blaine one of their "nasties" who was living in Vancouver, this without benefit of a court appearance. We have experienced that a number of times. That is certainly not acceptable under our system of justice. People have a right to a day in court. The RCMP has participated in such completely unacceptable activity.
With regard to the political situation, I do not think there are many Members of this House who have not been confronted with the problem of assisting refugees from regimes such as those in El Salvador and Chile. These people often have difficulties dealing with immigration. The immigration people say that if they have a criminal record or criminal charges pending in their country of origin they cannot enter this country. It would be very difficult to check with a regime such as that in Chile to determine whether a refugee has a criminal record.
It is dead wrong to allow the Cabinet of Canada to expand the list of countries which could enjoy the powers of this legislation without reference to Parliament. We should work at every stage of this Bill to stop that. Conceivably the Soviet
September 15, 1987

Union could request law enforcement action in Canada. That is not what Parliament has in mind with this legislation.
The Government has gone too far in the drafting of this Bill. If this Bill is passed at second reading, I would hope that an agreement could be made to drop that particular aspect.
Certain regimes consider activities to be criminal which bear no relation to criminal activity in Canada. These include free speech, protest and demonstration, and active involvement in trade union activities. These are rights which are worthy of guaranteeing constitutionally in a democratic country but are prohibited in regimes such as those in South Africa and Chile.
Under this legislation their law enforcement agencies could come to Canada and suggest that because an individual has committed that nature of a crime in their country they wish to enjoy the benefits of this legislation and have Canadian enforcement officials gather evidence against them and move to extradite them. This is the kind of thing that could result from the wide open, loose and sloppy drafting of this legislation.
We would have much more confidence in this legislation and the Government's application of it if we did not know that the Government is already involved with those regimes and very reluctant to criticize their most heinous and obscene actions. The Liberal Government opened trade with the regime in Chile which almost encourages its continuance. The Conservative Government has certainly done nothing to indicate that we should not expect the Chilean police forces to operate in Canada.

subtopic: MUTUAL LEGAL ASSISTANCE IN CRIMINAL MATTERS ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak on Bill C-58 with regard to mutual legal assistance in criminal matters between Canada and other countries. The "other countries" aspect will be the focus of my comments. My friends from Burnaby and Comox-Powell River have addressed, in particular, concerns involving Canada's relationship with the United States. That is understandable and always acceptable or forgivable depending upon one's perspective because we share the continent of North America with our powerful friends in the United States. Being a much smaller country in terms of population, we are always concerned about how Canadian interests will be defended by our Government vis-a-vis the United States.
I hardly need expand on the concerns that many Canadians have felt over the last three years as they have watched the present Government, and particularly the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), dealing with the U.S. President. They have wondered whether Canada's interests were not being sold out in those various contexts. I will not spend any more time on that this afternoon.
We are dealing with general legislation which raises concerns, which I want to explore, involving other countries. If there is any doubt about the validity of these observations I note that in the interpretation section of the Bill, where definitions are provided, "foreign state" is defined as "a state
that is a party to a treaty". Clearly that could be any state at all. Treaty means "a treaty, convention Or other international agreement that is in force and to which Gdnada is a party, the primary purpose of which is to provide for mutual legal assistance in criminal matters". In those two definitions in the interpretation section we have obvious evidence that this Bill could be applied to any country at all.
The provisions of this Bill, if it becomes law, will be quite far-reaching. I note in the next section the following statement in the first clause:
In the event of any inconsistency between the provisions of this Act and the provisions of another Act of Parliament, other than the provisions of an Act prohibiting the disclosure of information or prohibiting its disclosure except under certain conditions, the provisions of this Act prevail to the extent of the inconsistency.
I recognize, of course, that disclosure of information is a large part of criminal investigation, but there are in fact many other areas upon which it could touch. In all of those other areas this is the Act that will govern.
In lboking at Clause 6 of the Bill, within which are provisions for administrative arrangements, we will appreciate exactly how far-reaching this Bill is. We are told in of Clause 6(1):
Where there is no treaty between Canada and another state, the Secretary of State for External Affairs may, with the agreement of the Minister, enter into an administrative arrangement with that other state providing for legal assistance with respect to an investigatidh specified therein relating to an act that, if committed in Canada, would be an indictable offence.
In Clause 6(1) we have provision for the development of special arrangements in instances of countries that do not already have a treaty negotiated with Canada. The Bill, of course, does not have attached to it in a schedule a list of countries with which Canada has a treaty. Once passed, and if proclaimed, that would obviously be appended to it for Useful reference.
In Clause 6(1) authorization is being requested which would allow Canada to make arrangements with any country at all. That, of course, provides a basis for asking what the ramifications of this Bill might be, how far-reaching its powers might be, and what its consequences might be.
Shall I call it one o'clock, Mr. Speaker?
