subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-SENTENCE IN QUEBEC NATIONAL ASSEMBLY MURDER CASE-CALL FOR REFORM OF CRIMINAL LAW
ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-SENTENCE IN QUEBEC NATIONAL ASSEMBLY MURDER CASE-CALL FOR REFORM OF CRIMINAL LAW
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 know that you are well aware of the infamous case of Denis Lortie. You will recall that he is the man who, some three years ago, burst into the Quebec National Assembly carrying two sub-machine guns. Interestingly enough, we were just talking about gun control legislation. Mr. Lortie stormed into the Quebec National Assembly carrying two sub-machine guns, and within the space of some 45 minutes he had killed three innocent government employees and wounded some 13 others.
Adjournment Debate
At that time Lortie was convicted of first degree murder. He appealed that conviction, was granted a new trial, and finally in May of this year he pleaded guilty to three charges of second degree murder and nine charges of attempted murder. At that time he was sentenced by Mr. Justice Desjardins to a mandatory sentence of life imprisonment.
1 do not know what you think of, Mr. Speaker, when you hear the words "life in prison". What do they in fact mean in the case of Lortie? Well, in the Lortie case a life sentence means that he can apply for parole after 10 years. Not only can he apply for parole after 10 years, but it has been decided that the three years he has already spent in prison will be part of that 10 years. In fact, he can apply for parole, and will likely be out on parole after seven years at the most, and that for the murder, whether first or second degree, of three people, and a conviction on the charge of attempted murder of nine others.
Is that life in prison? It does not mean life imprisonment to me. 1 suspect it does not mean life imprisonment to you, Mr. Speaker. I venture to say that it does not mean life imprisonment to the vast majority of Canadians. I suspect that Canadians probably think life imprisonment means what happened in the case of Rudolf Hess. Once sentenced to life imprisonment, he did serve the rest of his natural life in prison. Of course, that is not what life imprisonment means in the case of the sentence of Denis Lortie, even though the judge used the words "life in prison".
I am sure, Mr. Speaker, you will recall another case that occurred very recently, the case of one Yves Trudeau. He has two nicknames. Some people know him as "Apache" Trudeau, and some people call him the "Mad Bumper". Yves Trudeau is a biker. He has confessed to murdering 43 people, and he is believed to have been involved in the murder of 40 others.
In exchange for turning police informer, Yves Trudeau was allowed to plead guilty to manslaughter. And he was sentenced, you guessed it, to life in prison. What does life in prison mean as far as Apache Trudeau is concerned? In his case, it means parole after seven years. This man admitted to killing 43 people and he is suspected of killing another 40, a total of 83 people. His sentence "life imprisonment" is seven years. Can you believe that, Mr. Speaker? Well, I cannot believe it. I know that by and large Canadians cannot believe it either.
Obviously we need something in the way of a major reform, at least in our sentencing in criminal cases and in our criminal justice system. The previous Government thought so too. It appointed something called the Canadian Sentencing Commission to study that problem. The Commission reported in March of this year. It said that there was a lack of public confidence in criminal sentencing, that there were great differences in sentencing for the same offences and that there were too many people being sent to jail for non-violent offences.

September 15, 1987
Adjournment Debate
The commission came up with a long list of recommendations which basically were aimed at restoring public confidence in our criminal justice system. How can we restore the confidence of the great Canadian public in our criminal justice system? I believe there are certain basic things we should be thinking of here. We should be wanting to make sure that a person who commits a serious offence pays a proper penalty for it by spending a substantial part of that person's life in prison.
1 believe that we should be looking at longer sentences for violent crimes, particularly murder. 1 believe that we should not be trivializing murder and other serious offences, particularly violent crimes, by rapid paroles. I believe that we should be trying to put more certainty into the sentencing procedure. We should limit the discretion that judges have in imposing sentences, not tying their hands altogether, but putting some definite limitations on their discretion and we should make them spell out specifically what sort of sentences they are imposing. We should not kid the troops by saying life imprisonment when we mean only 10, 15, 25 or even 7 years. We should make judges spell out specifically when parole of any sort is applicable and for how long a period. That is the sort of thing we should be doing.
I hope tonight that we will have from the Parliamentary Secretary some specific words on the subject, that he will tell us that that is what the Government will do and that it will do it fast. 1 hope he will not tell us, as reported in the newspaper yesterday, that although this report of the Sentencing Commission came out in March of this year that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) is not going to meet with his provincial counterparts on this until 1988. Surely the Government can do better than that.

speakeroldname: Mr. Francois Gerin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-SENTENCE IN QUEBEC NATIONAL ASSEMBLY MURDER CASE-CALL FOR REFORM OF CRIMINAL LAW
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for raising this issue because I must say at the outset that his remarks faithfully mirror the concerns of many Canadians in this respect. As it happens, they often find it hard to understand why an individual sentenced to five years should be paroled after a year and a half under conditions with which they are not familiar.
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Justice shares the concerns not only of the Hon. Member but of many Canadians, and I think he has made a commitment to take vigourous action to prevent crime, and violent crime more specifically. Perhaps the sanctions provided under the criminal Code ought to be more in line with the seriousness of the criminal act involved.
Last March 27 the Minister of Justice tabled in the House the report of the Canadian Sentencing Commission, a complex document of 592 pages containing 91 recommendations. We must take time to make an in-depth analysis of this report and
give it all the attention it deserves. The report recommendations have significant implications concerning every aspect of the criminal justice system, from police work to sentence serving. Its consequences for the provinces are particularly significant because they have jurisdiction over the administration of justice and the enforcement of many sanctions prescribed under the Criminal Code. This is why the provinces must have enough time to analyze the full impact of the report and have an opportunity to express their views at length. The Minister of Justice is therefore planning to have extensive consultations with the provincial Governments.
In addition, in view of the importance of this matter for all those involved with our criminal justice system, the Minister of Justice wants to consult all of them. These consultations should include the judiciary, the associations of defence counsels, the various provinces, the correctional authorities and certain organizations, such as the John Howard Society, which play an active role in the criminal justice system.
Finally, we must not forget the new draft of the Criminal Code prepared by the Law Reform Commission. Major reform proposals such as the new Code and the report of the Commission on sentencing cannot be examined independently. Comments about one must necessarily take the other into account.
However, in view of their importance as far as determining the direction to be given to the Canadian justice system, 1 can only say, Mr. Speaker, that whatever the time it takes to prepare a responsible reply to the recommendations of the Commission, this time will not be wasted.

subtopic: CANADA DEPOSIT INSURANCE CORPORATION-COVERAGE OF REGISTERED RETIREMENT SAVINGS PLANS-REQUEST FOR AMENDMENT TO LEGISLATION
CANADA DEPOSIT INSURANCE CORPORATION-COVERAGE OF REGISTERED RETIREMENT SAVINGS PLANS-REQUEST FOR AMENDMENT TO LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the 67,000 Canadians who entrusted their savings and RRSP funds to Principal Trust and its affiliated companies will lose $191 million as a result of the bankruptcies of these companies and particularly of First Investors and Associated Investors.
Speaking for the Government, the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin) has denied any real responsibility for this disaster by pointing out that with the exception of Principal Savings and Trust, whose depositors had their funds insured by the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation, all the other subsidiaries of that original trust company were established under the laws of the Province of Alberta and their depositors were not covered by CDIC. That claim is factually and legally correct.
There is at least one group of people who invested their savings in subsidiary companies and who had every right to expect that their money would be protected. I am referring to the thousands of people who put part or all of their savings into
September 15, 1987

registered retirement savings plans through these Principal subsidiaries.
These people were encouraged to put their money into these plans by federal legislation which told them that if they did so, they would not have to pay any income tax on that money until after retirement, when the plan would begin to give them an income which, together with the old age assistance and Canada Pension Plan, would permit them to live in relative comfort. Of course, at that time they would begin to pay income tax on that money.
It was not surprising that thousands of people put their RRSP funds into affiliated companies on the advice of the salesmen. The salesmen were paid a 3 per cent commission for making sales in these companies rather than the 1.5 per cent commission they were paid for sales in Principal Trust itself. Naturally they pushed the subsidiaries, and it is not surprising that they often did not warn their customers about the lack of protection in those companies.
Thousands have now had their retirement incomes wiped out. The tax they would have had to pay when they retired will also disappear. Surely it is time to amend the income tax law so that moneys put into RRSPs are required to be put into plans which are covered by CDIC.
The stories of some of the people who were hurt are just unbelievably sad. Let me put on record a few of the cases of which I have heard.
A 71-year-old man and his wife had over $17,000 in RRSPs and $20,000 in term certificates with First Investors. They were hoping for a small monthly income in their old age. Now everything is gone.
A senior citizen had $77,000 in RRSPs and term certificates with Associated Investors and First Investors. He now has only $200 in the bank. His entire life savings are gone.
A senior citizen had $12,000 in term certificates with First Investors. This amount was originally in Principal Savings and Trust Company and was insured. Without permission and with specific instructions not to do so, it was transferred over to the subsidiary companies that had no insurance.
An older gentleman had $15,000 in RRSPs. This represented his savings from over 20 years. He was told that the investment was guaranteed, but obviously it was not and his money is all or in large part gone.
A widower who is over 70 years invested all his life savings with First Investors. That money has disappeared.
I call on the Government to take its responsibilities seriously and act on behalf of ordinary Canadians who have been persuaded, and often duped, into investing in uninsured funds. The money involved was saved with great difficulty in order that they could live with some dignity and comfort in their retirement years. The least the Government can do is to amend
Adjournment Debate
the Income Tax Act with respect to RRSPs to ensure that the money invested in that way is covered by CDIC insurance. 1 call on the Government to take action and not delay any longer. Enough people have been seriously and grievously hurt.

speakeroldname: Mr. Francois Gerin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CANADA DEPOSIT INSURANCE CORPORATION-COVERAGE OF REGISTERED RETIREMENT SAVINGS PLANS-REQUEST FOR AMENDMENT TO LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation has always been to protect the deposits of Canadians against the loss of funds they could incur if the institution holding their deposits should go bankrupt.
Until now, full insurance coverage by the CDIC has been limited to certain types of deposits whose total amount does not exceed an amount set in the Act, which amount is now $60,000. The reason for this is that, contrary to small depositors, individuals and corporations having very large deposits or other types of investments normally have the knowledge and capacity to diversify their risks and avoid undue losses which could result from the bankruptcy of a financial institution. In other words, the purpose of deposit insurance is not to guarantee the types of investments made by corporations and wealthy individuals.
Members of this House will certainly agree that this reasoning still holds and applies just as well to RRSPs as to ordinary deposits. 1 especially wish to remind the Hon. Member that, if the Government maintained the present ceiling of $60,000 for full insurance coverage by the CDIC in Bill C-42, it was precisely because it wanted to make certain that the majority of small RRSP owners, that is those who invest only in regular deposit instruments and guaranteed investment certificates, would still be fully insured.
However, the solution proposed by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) is less than satisfactory. Under the Income Tax Act, Canadians are now entitled to choose among a large number of investment instruments with a savings retirement program associated with a RRSP. Any initiative to limit RRSP investments to insurable deposits under the Deposit Insurance Corporation Act would be too restrictive. It would probably result in the disappearance of self-managed RRSPs and reduce the possibility for RRSP owners of obtaining higher returns thanks to a more diversified investment strategy.
It is also important to provide similar protection when nonmember corporations are involved. There is now an investigation in Alberta on the misrepresentations which could have occured in relation with Principal Trust, which is a member institution of the Deposit Insurance Corporation, and its nonmember affiliates, First Investors and Associated Investors. In addition, the Government of Canada has already taken certain initiatives in Bills C-42 and C-56 to increase protection of consumers in general, and it is planning to take other such initiatives in the next legislative package on the reform of the financial sector.

September 15, 1987
Adjournment Debate
We also recognize the need to co-ordinate consumer protection measures in view of the sharing of jurisdiction over financial services. This is why this matter is also the subject of ongoing discussions with the provinces.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: THE CONSTITUTION-1987 CONSTITUTION ACCORD-LANGUAGE MINORITY GROUPS-REPRESENTATION OF LANGUAGE MINORITY GROUPS IN PUBLIC SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question I asked last June 5 had to do with the Constitutional Accord, more particularly with the provisions concerning the protection of the rights of official language minority groups. It will be recalled that the accord was tabled in the House on June 3. On June 4 I put a question to the Prime Minister, and I raised the issue again on June 5.
Mr. Speaker, I have already explained the problem we are faced with, either here in the House or before the Special Joint Committee on the Constitutional Accord. I have had an opportunity to explain the problem facing minorities.
The only thing mentioned in the accord is the obligation of the federal Parliament and the provincial legislatures to protect the rights of official language minority groups. There is no question of promotion. To me, that is insufficient.
Protecting the present situation is tantamount to protecting the status quo, which is just another way of saying that, because of the rapid rate of assimilation which will be threatening us in the coming years, we of the Canadian Diaspora, it threatens with disappearance groups who are important for the survival of this country, our Canada, with two official languages.
We believe that the Meech Lake Accord must be amended so as to include, in addition to the notion of protection of the linguistic duality, the notion of promotion of that duality. This is a crucial aspect, especially for the francophone minorities outside Quebec.
If we are prepared to include in our Constitution the notion of linguistic duality, as suggested in the accord and as a fundamental characteristic of Canada, it seems to me the least we can say is that we must make sure that this fundamental characteristic will endure and be the subject of some kind of promotion on the part of both federal and provincial government levels. This requires the assurance that there will be promotion in addition to preservation.
Yet, notwithstanding all the evidence heard by the special committee to urge the Government to amend the accord, it has been to no avail. The Prime Minister keeps saying that the accord cannot be amended lest it be compromised.
But what was the specific purpose of this new constitutional round? It was to redress the situation where Quebec was not a full-fledged member of the Canadian constitutional family. Therefore, negotiations were based on the five proposals submitted by the Quebec Government: first, the specific
recognition of Quebec as a distinct society; second, the guarantee that Quebec's powers in the area of immigration will be widened; third, a limitation to the Canadian Government's spending powers; four, a review of the constitutional amendment process, including the recognition of Quebec's veto right; and five, Quebec's involvement in the appointment of Supreme Court justices.
We in the Liberal Party support all those principles. But as our Leader the Right Hon. John Turner stated last week, and I quote:
We want to provide better protection to official language minorities by ensuring that the Canadian Government has a responsibility not only to protect, but also to promote the rights of official language minorities across Canada. Provinces also would have an opportunity to commit themselves not only to the protection but also to the promotion of our linguistic duality.
Mr. Speaker, we accept the Meech Lake Agreement because we accept Quebec's five claims. However, I cannot see how the amendment we are proposing on the obligation, at least at the federal level, to promote language duality might conflict with Quebec's demands. In my view, this creates no problem as far as adopting the Meech Lake Agreement is concerned.
Moreover, I cannot see how this amendment can be rejected by other provinces because only those that would want to would be committing themselves. If they do not want to, no problem, they will not have to. The idea would be that the federal level, the Canadian Parliament would undertake to promote official languages across the country and that provinces in due course, when they feel like it, would do the same.
If they are generous enough towards their minority and if they really believe in what they signed when they recognized this language duality as a basic feature of Canada, then they could and should prove their good intentions by becoming promoters of that language duality.
To me, Mr. Speaker, as to many experts we heard here and in committee, there is no problem with that amendment. The Government would have us believe that we want to foul up the Agreement. That is not true! We wholeheartedly want Quebec to join Canada again in an atmosphere of good will.
If there are problems, and I feel that I have just demonstrated that there are none with the addition of the word "promotion", those who are saying that there are problems should provide proof of that: the onus is on them, not on us.
A newspaperman wrote this morning in the Montreal Gazette-and I was quite surprised to read that Mr. William Johnson could write anything like that-and I quote in English from the Montreal Gazette of September 12, 1987:
So the come-from-behind Liberals propose to give to Ottawa and all the provinces the responsibility for "promoting" as well as preserving minority language rights and linguistic duality.
September 15, 1987



Mr. Speaker, I do not accept the "come-from-behind" label. The day following the Meech Lake Constitutional Accord, 1 raised in the House the issue of adding promotion to the Accord in addition to ensuring the protection of minorities.
I suggest, therefore, that Mr. Johnson should read these documents and make sure he realizes that what we want is neither more nor less, and that if we say that there will be protection, Mr. Speaker, it is quite normal to say that there must be also promotion if we are really serious about this Accord.
Mr. Speaker, the Government which resists any amendment refuses to share the legal opinions it has received from many specialists on the real impact the definition of "distinct society" may have.
Mr. Speaker, are the rights of women, natives, linguistic minorities truly subject to the Charter of Rights and Freedoms? 1 think so, but the Government adds: We have authorities, legal opinions which support this position.
If such legal opinions exist, why does the Government not share them with us and tell us exactly where this difficult question which is the subject of a national debate comes from?
The Government has recognized that promoting a linguistic duality is essential. 1 simply refer you to the Official Languages Act which incorporates in a Parliament's statute the obligation for the Federal Government to get involved in promotion.
Well, we are all aware that a statute may be amended, but a constitution is strong and resistant. All we want is: Make sure that not only the constitutional concept is accepted and enshrined, that the Federal Government is really committed to preserve the French reality outside Quebec and the English reality inside Quebec, but that it is obligated to promote this concept.
I feel this is not difficult to understand and does not seem to affect the Meech Lake Accord in anyway, except that it will give something very strong and reinforce the obligation for the Federal Government not only in a statutory fashion, but also in a Constitutional fashion, also to promote preservation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: THE CONSTITUTION-1987 CONSTITUTION ACCORD-LANGUAGE MINORITY GROUPS-REPRESENTATION OF LANGUAGE MINORITY GROUPS IN PUBLIC SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not understand anything anymore.
My colleague has been promoting the official languages, his record is impressive in that respect and I commend him for that. But now he is getting mixed up and tripping over carpet flowers. Listen, all he has to do is look it up in the official
Adjournment Debate
languages measure which was tabled recently, Bill C-72, which says in so many words that the Government will have to promote this Canadian duality in its institutions. But that is already a fait accompli. Where my friend gets all mixed up is when he starts talking about the Meech Lake Accord. That is where he trips, falls down, and does not know how to get back on his feet. I can understand him to a certain extent because to them and to Quebec, what did distinct society mean in 1982? In 1982, "distinct society" meant that Quebec was being left right out of the Constitutionbal Accord, it simply was not there. What you did was unspeakable, and you signed that without Quebec.
Today we have a Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) who gets along with the ten provincial premiers, he comes up with an accord, you admit it is a nice accord but in fact you are saying it lacks this and lacks that. Everything was lacking when you signed the accord because Quebec was left out, half of Canada was missing, one of the founding peoples was missing , everything was missing. And today you are telling us that we ought to add promotion .. . not the other provinces but only Quebec. But it is included in Bill C-72.
Well, make up your mind on this question, make up your mind about the Meech Lake Accord, take a definite position, stop straddling the issue. The Meech Lake Accord is the perfect constitutional accord for 1987. In 1995, in 1992, at the next constitutional round we can amend it, Mr. Speaker. Do not back both horses. It is a perfect accord. It is a perfect accord today, it is endorsed by nearly all Canadians.
The Liberals simply cannot make up their mind. Stop confusing people.
